checklist: Open M_Chair from the Starter Content. Find the mask texture T_Chair_M and see how each channel (R, G, B, A) drives a different part of the chair.
In an image tool, paint four black-and-white masks for one of your own meshes. Put one mask in each channel and export them as one file named T_MyProp_Masks.
Import T_MyProp_Masks. Open it in the Texture Editor, uncheck sRGB, and set Compression Settings to Masks.

Create a material named M_MyProp. Add a Texture Sample node for the mask texture and check that its Sampler Type is Masks. This matches the Masks compression setting of the texture, and the editor usually sets it for you. With any other Sampler Type the material shows an error.
Use the R channel as a metal mask and the G channel as an emissive (glow) mask. Use the B channel as the Alpha of a Lerp node that blends between two Vector Parameters for the color.
Make a Material Instance named MI_MyProp_Red and change only the color parameters in it. Apply it to the mesh.

Switch to Modeling Mode with Shift+5. If the mode is missing, enable the Modeling Tools Editor Mode plugin first. Find the four panels: Tool Category, Tool Palette, Tool Properties and Quick Settings.
Choose Create, then Box. Set Output Type to Static Mesh and click in the level to place the box. Name the asset SM_ModelTest.

Choose Model, then PolyGroup Edit. Select one face and Extrude it, which pushes the face outward. Then Bevel one edge, which cuts the sharp edge into a small slope. Click Accept. Press Ctrl+Z once and see what is undone.

Place any Starter Content prop in the level and select it. Choose XForm, then Duplicate, and click Accept. This makes a new mesh asset that is a copy, so the original prop stays as it is. With the copy selected, choose Mesh, then Simplify, reduce it to about half the triangles, and click Accept.
In the viewport, turn on Show > Advanced > Mesh Edges. Use Attribs > Inspect on the simplified copy and look at the result. Then use Attribs > Inspect Collision.
Open Quick Settings and turn off Combined Gizmo. Note how the gizmo changes.

Duplicate the FX_Smoke emitter asset that you saved in quest TAQ56, move the copy to a new folder, and rename it FX_Sparks_Smoke. Right-click it and choose Create Niagara System. Name the system SparksSystem and drag it into your level.

In FX_Sparks_Smoke, find Emitter State and set Life Cycle Mode to System, and set Spawn Rate to 20. In Initialize Particle, make the lifetime random from 2 to 3 and make the color dark gray (0.3). Make Add Velocity point mostly upward, with Z from 25 to 35, and set the sphere radius of Shape Location to 5.
In the Particle Update group of the smoke emitter, open Scale Color. Turn off Scale RGB, and give Scale Alpha the Smooth Ramp Down shape so the smoke fades out. Set Acceleration Force to Z 20.

Add a second emitter from the Simple Sprite Burst template and name it FX_SparkBurst. In the Render group, set the material to M_Spark, which is in the Starter Content under Particles, then Materials. Delete Sprite Burst Instantaneous, set Life Cycle Mode to System, add a Spawn Rate of 50, set Lifetime to 0.2, and set the RGB of Scale Color to 2, 6, 25.

Add a third Simple Sprite Burst emitter and name it FX_Sparks_Radial. Set the material to M_Radial_Gradient, from the same Starter Content folder, and set Alignment to Velocity Aligned, so each spark points the way it moves. Use a Spawn Rate of 500, a random lifetime from 0.2 to 0.7, and Add Velocity with a random range where Z goes from 300 to 500.

In the Particle Update group of FX_Sparks_Radial, add Gravity Force with Z -4500, Drag with 1.7, and Collision with Restitution 0.4 and Friction 0.2. Remove Scale Color, and add Scale Sprite Size by Speed with a Velocity Threshold of 2000.
Look at the effect in the level and adjust one value that you do not like, for example the gravity or the spawn rate of the radial emitter.
TAQ55.brief: A good spark effect is not one emitter but several that work together. An emitter is the part of a Niagara system that creates one kind of particle. Here you combine three: soft smoke, a bright flash at the center, and fast sparks that fly out, fall and bounce. In this quest you build a system with these three emitters, starting from the smoke emitter of quest TAQ56.

TAQ57.brief: You do not have to build every effect from zero. If you copy an emitter that already works and change a few values, you get a new effect in much less time. In this quest you copy the smoke emitter from quest TAQ56 and change its speed, color, size and forces until it looks like steam.
checklist: Right-click the FX_Smoke emitter asset from quest TAQ56 and choose Duplicate Emitter. Move the copy to a new folder and rename it FX_Steam.
Right-click FX_Steam and choose Create Niagara System. This makes a new system that already contains the emitter. Name the system Steam and drag it into your level.
In Emitter Update, find Emitter State and set Life Cycle Mode to System. Then set Spawn Rate to 30.

In Initialize Particle, set the lifetime range to 3 to 7, the color to white (1, 1, 1) and the sprite size to 100 to 200. Set Add Velocity so that it pushes the particles sideways and up (X 16 to 32, Y -5 to 5, Z 35 to 50). Set the sphere radius to 20.

In Particle Update, give Acceleration Force a random range with a minimum of X 25, Y -10, Z 15 and a maximum of X 55, Y 10, Z 25. In Scale Color, pick the Pulse Out curve shape, which makes the steam fade in and then fade out.
Add a Drag module, which slows the particles down. When the 'unmet dependencies' error appears, click Fix Issue so that Niagara moves the module to the correct place. Set Drag to 0.8.
Make a new material named M_TA_CustomBlur. Add a Custom node to the graph. You can find it with the right-click search or in the Custom category of the Palette.

Select the Custom node. In its Inputs array, add four inputs named Tex, UV, r and dist. Set Output Type to a 3-channel float. Copy the blur code from the Custom Material Expressions page that is linked on this quest, and paste it into the Code field.
Connect a Texture Object node to Tex, a TexCoord node to UV, and two Scalar Parameters to r and dist. Set Description to 'Box Blur' so that the title of the node is clear.
Add one extra output to the node with Additional Outputs, for example a luminance (brightness) value, and use it somewhere in the graph.

Build a second, simple effect two times: once in a Custom node and once with built-in nodes (for example Sin, Multiply by a parameter, and Add). Compare the two instruction counts in the Stats panel. A lower count means a cheaper material.
Write 3 short lines that say when you would keep the Custom node here, and when you would replace it with nodes.

TAQ1.done_when: Send one image that shows 7 labeled views from the same camera (Lit, Unlit, Wireframe, Detail Lighting, Lighting Only, Shader Complexity and Light Complexity). Add one line about the most expensive object you found.

checklist: Open Edit > Plugins, look in the Animation section, enable the Deformer Graph plugin and restart. Use the mannequin from the Third Person template.
Select the character in the level. In the Details panel, enable Mesh Deformer and create a new Deformer Graph asset named DG_Twist. Open the asset and set its Mesh property to the mannequin.

In the Update Graph, add a Skeletal Mesh Component Binding node. Connect these nodes to it: Write Skinned Mesh, Execute Skinned Mesh (with Domain set to Vertex), Scene Data (for Time) and Skinned Mesh (for Position, Tangent X and Tangent Z).

Add a Custom Compute Kernel node. In its Details panel, add the inputs Num Threads (Int Vector 3, Parameter), Twist, Start, End and Time (Float, Parameter), Position (Vector 3, Vertex x1), and Tangent X and Tangent Y (Vector 4, Vertex x1). Add the outputs Out Position (Vector 3) and OutTangentX and OutTangentZ (Vector 4), all set to Vertex x1. Set Execution Domain to Vertex, then click Save and Compile.
Check that the Declarations tab lists ReadPosition, ReadTwist and WriteOutPosition. Then paste the HLSL twist program from the page into the Shader Text tab.

Connect the read nodes to the inputs of the kernel, and connect the outputs of the kernel to Write Skinned Mesh. Add three Float Constant nodes: Twist 180, Start 0 and End 100. Click Save and Compile, and watch the character twist in the viewport and in the level.
Replace the Twist constant with a Deformer Graph Variable named TwistAmount, so that the value can be changed from outside the graph. Set it to 45 and compare.
Create an Editor Utility Blueprint named EUB_ActorActions with the parent class ActorActionUtility.
Add a function named Set Material Slot 0 with two inputs: a Material Object Reference and a Boolean named 'Only Static Meshes'. Keep Call In Editor checked.
In the function, use Get Selection Set to get the selected actors, loop over them, and set the material on their Static Mesh Component. Also handle the case where the material input is empty.
Open Class Defaults and add Static Mesh Actor to Supported Classes, so that the action does not appear on lights or cameras.
Add a Custom Event named 'Snap To Ground' with Call In Editor checked. It does a line trace (an invisible ray) down from each selected actor and moves the actor to the point that the ray hits.

Compile and save. Then select 3 Static Mesh Actors in the viewport, right-click them, and run both actions from the Scripted Actor Actions sub-menu. The documentation page calls this menu Scripted Actions.
TAQ82.done_when: Send a screenshot of the Scripted Actor Actions sub-menu on a selected actor, a screenshot of the input popup window for Set Material Slot 0, and a screenshot of the actors after both actions ran.

checklist: Open Edit > Plugins, look in the Physics category, enable ChaosVehiclesPlugin and restart the editor. Get a vehicle skeletal mesh that has wheel bones. The documentation uses the Buggy from the Vehicle Game sample and says to find it in the Epic Games Launcher under Learn. In newer Launchers the sample projects are on the Samples tab. A free vehicle from Fab also works.

Create two Blueprints from the class ChaosVehicleWheel. Name one BP_WheelFront, with Affected by Steering on and Axle Type set to front. Name the other BP_WheelRear, with Affected by Handbrake and Affected by Engine on. Set Wheel Radius to match the size of the visible wheel in cm (58 for the Buggy).

Create the physics asset: right-click the skeletal mesh, choose Create, then Physics Asset, then Create and Assign, with Single Convex Hull. In the Physics Asset Editor, select all wheel bones, set Primitive Type to Sphere and click Re-generate Bodies. Then select the suspension bones and choose Collision, then No Collision.
Create a Curve Float asset named TorqueCurve (under Miscellaneous, then Curve). Give it the shape of an upside-down U, where X is the engine RPM and Y is the torque, the turning force of the engine.

Create an Animation Blueprint named ABP_Vehicle with the parent class VehicleAnimationInstance and the Skeleton of the vehicle. In the AnimGraph, connect Mesh Space Ref Pose to Wheel Controller for WheeledVehicle, then to Component To Local, then to Output Pose. If the mesh has suspension bones, add Look At nodes so that they follow the wheel joints.

Create a Blueprint named BP_Vehicle from WheeledVehiclePawn. Set the Skeletal Mesh and the Anim Class, and turn on Simulate Physics. On the Vehicle Movement Component, fill Wheel Setups with a Wheel Class and a Bone Name for each wheel (FL, FR, BL, BR), and set the Torque Curve External Curve to TorqueCurve. Add a Spring Arm and a Camera.

Make a Game Mode with BP_Vehicle as the Default Pawn, and set it as GameMode Override in World Settings. Connect your input to Set Throttle Input and Set Steering Input, and press Play. Watch the wheels spin and steer.
Open Edit > Plugins, look in the Animation section, and enable the Skeletal Mesh Editing Tools plugin. Restart the editor.

Pick a simple static mesh prop that should bend, for example an antenna, a lamp arm or a tall cylinder made in Modeling Mode. Right-click it in the Content Browser, choose Convert to Skeletal Mesh, and pick Create New for the Skeleton. Name the result SK_Antenna.

Open the new Skeletal Mesh SK_Antenna, not the Skeleton asset. In the toolbar of the Skeletal Mesh Editor, click Editing Tools and choose the Skeleton mode. With the Edit Skeleton tool in Add mode (N), select the root bone and drag three new bones up the prop, one after the other. Click Accept.

Select the three new bones together and rename the first one to seg_##1, so that they become seg_001, seg_002 and seg_003. In Edit mode, use Orient with Primary X and Orient Children turned on, so that all bones point the same way.

Switch to the Skin mode and run Bind Skin with Binding Type set to Geodesic Voxel and Max Influences set to 4. Then open Edit Weights, select a bone, and paint with the Brush in Add mode. Hold Shift to Relax (smooth) the weights where two bones meet, and click Accept.
Test the rig: select seg_002 in the Skeleton Tree, rotate it with the gizmo, and check that the prop bends smoothly. If the bend looks bad, go back and paint the weights again.
Open a level that uses Lumen GI and Lumen reflections. Add a few smooth surfaces with low roughness, for example a floor with a roughness of 0.2.
Run the console command stat GPU. Write down the times of the three Lumen passes: Lumen Scene Lighting, Lumen Screen Probe Gather and Lumen Reflections.
Run r.Lumen.AsyncCompute 0 and read the Lumen timings again. Note the difference. With this setting off, the numbers show the cost of Lumen alone.
Switch the viewport to the Performance Overview view mode. Find the pixels that trace their own reflection rays.
In a Post Process Volume, lower Max Roughness To Trace, and watch how the Lumen Reflections time changes.
Try r.Lumen.Reflections.DownsampleFactor 2, and note the change in the timing and in the image.
Set sg.GlobalIlluminationQuality and sg.ReflectionQuality to 3 (Epic), then to 2 (High), and then to 1 (Medium). Record the times of the three Lumen passes for each setting.
Open a heavy level. Run the console commands stat unit and stat unitgraph. Confirm that the DynRes line says that dynamic resolution is off.
In a Blueprint (for example in the Level Blueprint on BeginPlay), call Get Game User Settings and then Set Dynamic Resolution Enabled with the value true.
In the console, set r.DynamicRes.OperationMode 1 and r.DynamicRes.FrameTimeBudget 16.6, and then play. Read the primary and secondary screen percentages on the DynRes line.
Run stat raw. Watch the curve of the primary screen percentage drop during a camera cut or a big effect.
Stop playing. Move the Screen Percentage slider of the editor viewport to 50, and look closely at a thin object such as a fence or a grill.

Compare the same object at 50 percent with and without a temporal upscaler. In UE5 the default anti-aliasing method, Temporal Super Resolution (TSR), is the temporal upscaler. Type r.AntiAliasingMethod 1 in the console to switch to FXAA, which has no temporal upscaling, and take a screenshot. Then type r.AntiAliasingMethod 4 to go back to TSR and take a second one. The older command r.TemporalAA.Upsampling only applies to the TAA method.
Run profileGPU once at 100 percent and once at 50 percent. Note which passes get cheaper.
TAQ107.done_when: Send a screenshot of stat unitgraph that shows the DynRes line with a changing primary screen percentage, plus two viewport screenshots of a thin object at 50 percent, one with the temporal upscaler (TSR) and one without it (FXAA).

checklist: Install RenderDoc from renderdoc.org. Confirm that the RenderDoc plugin is enabled in your project (it is on by default).
Open Project Settings, then Plugins, then RenderDoc, and enable Auto attach on startup. Restart the editor and find the RenderDoc icon in the upper-right corner of the Level Viewport.
Open a level that has at least 20 meshes and one Niagara system. Run the console command stat unit and write down the GPU time in ms.
Click the RenderDoc Capture button in the Level Viewport. Open the capture in RenderDoc and find the event list, which shows the draw events of the frame.

In the Event Browser of RenderDoc, click the clock button to show the duration of each event, because the times are hidden at first. Find the three most expensive events in the capture. Note which pass each one belongs to (base pass, shadows, post process, and so on). A pass is one stage of drawing the frame.
Write a short table with the pass name, the time, and which content in your level causes it.
Turn Auto attach on startup off again if you do not need it every day.
Open an expensive material that you already have. If you have none, build one named M_TA_Tiered with a detail normal, a parallax-style UV trick and two extra texture layers.

Add a QualitySwitch node before the Normal input. Connect the full detail network to High, a cheaper version (base normal only) to Default, and a flat normal constant to Low. Leave the Medium and Epic inputs empty. An empty input uses what is connected to Default.
Add a second QualitySwitch node on Base Color. Here High keeps all layers, and Low uses only one texture sample.
Add a FeatureLevelSwitch node on the whole Base Color result. Connect a single static texture to ES3.1 and connect the switched network to Default.

In the viewport, open the Performance and Scalability menu and change Material Quality Level between Low, Medium and High. In older versions this setting is under Settings in the main toolbar. Take a screenshot of the same mesh at each level.
Open the Stats panel and write down the instruction count that the editor shows. Write one line about which branch you think the editor preview is showing.
Create a Niagara Emitter asset named FXE_TA_HitBase (the Fountain template is fine). Set a Spawn Rate, a Lifetime range and a Sprite Size range that you like, and save it.

Open FXE_TA_HitBase. In Emitter Properties, under Asset Options, set Library Visibility so that the emitter shows in the library. Categories in the Niagara Asset Browser come from tags, so create a Niagara Asset Tag Definitions asset with a tag named TA Hits. Then right-click the emitter in the Content Browser, choose Manage Tags, and give it that tag.
Right-click FXE_TA_HitBase in the Content Browser and choose Create Niagara System. Name the system FXS_TA_HitVariants.

In FXS_TA_HitVariants, right-click the System Overview and choose Add Emitter. Add FXE_TA_HitBase two more times, so the system has three emitters. Rename the three emitters to Concrete, Glass and Wood.
In Glass, override the color in Initialize Particle. In Wood, add a Gravity Force module. Leave Concrete unchanged.
Open FXE_TA_HitBase again and change its Spawn Rate. Go back to FXS_TA_HitVariants and confirm that all three children picked up the new rate but kept their own overrides.
In one child, click the reset arrow next to an overridden value to set it back to the value of the parent.
TAQ63.done_when: Send a screenshot of FXS_TA_HitVariants with the three child emitters visible and one override arrow visible in the stack. Also send a second screenshot of the Niagara Asset Browser that shows FXE_TA_HitBase with your TA Hits tag.

GDQ77.done_when: Send two screenshots. The first shows FXS_HitBurst open in the Niagara Editor with the Emitter Update and Particle Spawn modules. The second shows the Blueprint graph with Spawn System at Location connected to the Impact Point of the trace. Say which spawn node followed the moving target.
checklist: Right-click in the Content Browser, choose FX, then Niagara System. Pick the Simple Sprite Burst template and name the system FXS_HitBurst. Rename the emitter to HitBurst.
In Emitter Update, in Emitter State, set Loop Behavior to Once and Loop Duration to 1. In Spawn Burst Instantaneous, set Spawn Count to 12.

In Particle Spawn, set Lifetime to a random value from 0.2 to 0.4. Add Shape Location with Shape Primitive set to Sphere and a small radius. Then add the module Add Velocity from the Velocity group, with Velocity Mode set to From Point and a speed of about 300. If the stack shows an error, click Fix Issue.
In Particle Update, add the Drag module from the Forces group and set Drag to 5. Keep Scale Color, so that the burst fades out.

In BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, where your punch trace hits, call Spawn System at Location with System Template FXS_HitBurst at the Impact Point and with Auto Destroy on. Rotate it so that it faces along the Impact Normal.

Make a second call with Spawn System Attached, attached to the mesh of the hit actor. Set Attach Point Name to a socket or a bone, and set Location Type to Keep Relative Offset. Move the target and note which burst follows it.
Drag FXS_HitBurst into the level one time, next to the character, to check its size. Then remove it.

Open an outdoor level that has a low area. Place an Exponential Height Fog, enable Volumetric Fog on it, and keep the Fog Density low. Give the Directional Light a Volumetric Scattering Intensity of 1.

Create a material named M_FogSphere and set Material Domain to Volume. Make a SphereMask that compares Absolute World Position with Particle Position and takes its radius from Particle Radius. Multiply it by a tiling noise texture and connect the result to Extinction. Connect a constant 1 to Albedo.
Create a simple Niagara sprite system named FXS_LowFog with a few large, slow particles. Assign M_FogSphere in its Sprite Renderer. Place the system in the low area.
Save a camera bookmark. Take a screenshot of the valley with FXS_LowFog hidden and another with it visible, both from that same bookmark.
Place a Spot Light in the fog. Turn Cast Volumetric Shadow off and on, and read stat GPU or profilegpu for both cases.
Set Scattering Distribution on the fog to 0.9. Look toward the sun and then away from it. Then set it back to the default.
Add a light that flickers, driven by a Blueprint or by Sequencer. If it leaves trails in the fog, set its Volumetric Scattering Intensity to 0.
Make a Niagara system named FXS_Fountain from a simple emitter template. For example, use Fountain, or Simple Sprite Burst with a Spawn Rate module added.
In the Parameters panel, add a User parameter of type float named SpawnRate, and a User parameter of type Linear Color named TintColor.
Link the Spawn Rate module to User SpawnRate, and link the particle Color to User TintColor. Give both parameters sensible default values.
Place FXS_Fountain in a level. Select it and check that both values show in the Details panel under Override Parameters.

Make a Blueprint named BP_FountainController that has a Niagara component, or a reference to the system you placed. On a key press, call Set Niagara Variable (Float) for SpawnRate and Set Niagara Variable (LinearColor) for TintColor.
Start Play in Editor and press the key. Confirm that the effect changes its rate and color, and that you did not have to edit the Niagara asset.

Build a material named M_Master_Prop with clear parameters, such as a color tint, a roughness value, and a texture switch or a scale. Put the parameters in groups and give them names that artists will understand.
Make at least 3 Material Instances from it, with names that start with MI_, that look clearly different. Use them on props in one small scene.

Build one Niagara system, with a name that starts with FXS_, that has at least one User parameter (for example SpawnRate or TintColor). You may drive it from an MPC value instead. MPC is short for Material Parameter Collection.
Make one Blueprint, with a name that starts with BP_, that changes that value during play. It can use a key press, a trigger or a timer.
If you use an MPC, let the same value also change M_Master_Prop, so that the props and the effect react together.
Write a short usage note for artists. It should list each parameter, its safe range, and which Blueprint call drives the effect.
Record a short clip, or take before and after screenshots, in Play In Editor (PIE).
Make a Niagara system named FXS_BouncingSparks that uses a fountain emitter. Place it above a floor and a box in a test level.
In the Particle Update group, click the + button and choose Collision, then Collision, to add the Collision module. Keep it right before the solver module in the stack.
Set Bounce Restitution to about 0.4 and Friction to about 0.2. Restitution controls how much speed a particle keeps after a bounce. Check that the sparks bounce off the floor.
Duplicate the emitter. On the copy, open Emitter Properties and set Sim Target to GPU. Keep the first emitter on CPU.
On the GPU copy, try the options of GPU Collision Type. Turn the camera so the floor leaves the screen, and note what changes.
Write 3 lines that say what each version used to find surfaces, and which version you would ship for this effect.
In the Content Drawer, choose FX, then Niagara System, then New system from selected emitters, and pick Simple Sprite Burst. Name the system FXS_RibbonTrail and drag it into a level.
In the Render group, delete the Sprite Renderer and add a Ribbon Renderer. Pick DefaultRibbonMaterial as its material. To find this material, turn on Show Engine Content and Show Plugin Content.
In the Emitter Update group, set the Life Cycle Mode of Emitter State to System. Then add a Spawn Rate module with a rate of about 100.
In the Particle Spawn group, set Lifetime, Color and Ribbon Width. Add a Shape Location module set to Ring / Disk and an Add Velocity module set to From Point, so that the ribbon spirals.
In the Particle Update group, remove Scale Color. Add an Acceleration Force module with a negative Z value so that the ribbon falls.
Try one setting of the Ribbon Renderer, either UV0 Tiling Distance or Tessellation, and note what changed.
In the Content Browser, create a Niagara module script named NMS_TA_PullToPoint. Open it in the Script Editor.

Add two Module Inputs named TargetPosition and Strength. Read Particle.Position, calculate the direction to the target and store it in a Module Local (a value that exists only inside this module), and then write a new Particle.Velocity.

In Script Details, set Module Usage Bitmask to the particle scripts, and fill in a Category, a Description and Keywords. Turn on Expose to Library so the module shows up when you add modules. Then click Compile.
Add the module to the Particle Update group of a system named FXS_TA_PullTest. Check that the particles move toward the target.
In the module script, click Versioning and enable it. Mark version 1.0 as the exposed version.

Add a new minor version. In it, add an input named Falloff and write a Change Description. Then set this version as exposed and visible. In FXS_TA_PullTest, switch the module to the new version from the Selection panel.
Create a Niagara System named FXS_TA_Embers from the Fountain template and drag it into your level.

In Particle Spawn, open Initialize Particle. Enable Sprite Rotation and set the mode to Direct Angle (Degrees). Then click the dropdown arrow next to the value, choose Dynamic Inputs, then Random Range Float, and set the range from -10 to 30.
In Add Velocity, click the dropdown arrow next to the value and choose Dynamic Inputs, then Random Range Vector. Give it a small range for X and Y and a larger range for Z.
In Particle Update, open Scale Color. Turn off Scale RGB, and apply the Smooth Ramp Down template to the Scale Alpha curve so each particle fades out over its life.
Add a Scale Sprite Size module to Particle Update. Set Scale Factor to a curve so that particles grow and then shrink. Then open Window > Curves and edit the same curve in that panel.
Chain two dynamic inputs: on any float value, pick a dynamic input, and then pick another dynamic input on one of its own inputs. Note the result.
Find the Library Only checkbox in the dynamic input list. Uncheck it and see which extra entries appear in the list.

Create a Niagara System named FXS_TA_Fireworks with an emitter named Rocket (CPU sim, from the Sprite Burst or Fountain template). Give the rockets a lifetime of about 2 s and a strong upward velocity.
In the Rocket emitter, open Emitter Properties and enable Requires Persistent ID. Events need this so that each particle can be identified.
In the Particle Update group of Rocket, click the + button. Under Events, add Generate Location Event and Generate Death Event.

Add a second emitter named Trail. Click the + button next to Emitter Properties and add an Event Handler. Set Source to the location event of Rocket, set Execution Mode to Spawned Particles and set Spawn Number to 3. Then add a Receive Location Event module.

Add a third emitter named Explosion. Add an Event Handler with Source set to the death event of Rocket and a Spawn Number of about 60, and add a Receive Death Event module. Give the explosion particles a short lifetime and a random sphere velocity.
As a test, set Execution Mode to Every Particle on the Trail handler and watch what happens. Then set it back to Spawned Particles.
Optional: add a Collision module to Rocket and then a Generate Collision Event. Make the explosion also start when a rocket hits something.
Create a Niagara System named FXS_TA_MeshSpawn from the Fountain template. Remove the modules Add Velocity in Cone and Shape Location.
In Particle Spawn, add a Static Mesh Location module. Set its Static Mesh data interface to a Starter Content mesh (Shape_Sphere is fine). Confirm that particles appear on the surface of the mesh.

Add a second emitter. In its Particle Spawn group, add a Skeletal Mesh Location module and point the data interface at a skeletal mesh from your project (the mannequin works). Try both bone/socket sampling and surface sampling.

In the second emitter, replace the Sprite Renderer with a Mesh Renderer, which draws each particle as a 3D mesh. Set Particle Mesh to a small mesh. Enable Override Materials and add a material that has the Niagara Mesh Particles flag checked.
In Initialize Particle, set the Sprite attributes to Unset, because a Mesh Renderer does not use them. Set Mesh Scale Mode to Random Uniform with a small range.
On the Mesh Renderer, set Facing Mode to Velocity and compare the result with Default.
Place the system in the level next to the source mesh, and check that the particles follow its surface.
Open Edit > Plugins and search for Niagara. Enable Niagara Fluids, accept the Beta warning and restart the editor.
Right-click in the Content Drawer and choose Niagara System. Under Niagara Fluids, then 3D Gas, pick Grid3D_Gas_Explosion. Name the system FXS_TA_GasExplosion and drag it into the level.

Select the system in the level. In the Details panel, under Override Parameters, set WorldSpaceSize to 300, 300, 600 and ResolutionMaxAxis to 300. Turn ShowOverlays off and on again to restart the explosion.
Add a Sphere above the explosion, inside the bounds of the simulation. Add an actor tag named collider to the sphere, and watch the gas flow around it.

Open the system. In Grid3D_Gas_CONTROLS_Emitter, open Emitter Summary. Set Density Dissipation to 3.0, Temperature Dissipation to 1.5, Velocity Dissipation to 0.8 and Temperature Buoyancy to 3.5. Dissipation is how fast a value fades away, and buoyancy makes hot gas rise.
In the Render section, set Render Density Gain to 0.5. Switch Render Temperature to Curve and edit the color curve.
Note the frame time with ResolutionMaxAxis at 300 and then at 150, and write both numbers down.
Create a Niagara System named FXS_Fountain from the Default System and add the Fountain emitter to it. Rename the emitter to Fountain-R.
Create a second system from the FountainLightweight template and name it FXS_Fountain_LW. Rename its emitter to Fountain-LW, set Spawn Rate to 300 and set Scale Color to red.
Make a new Basic level named NiagaraLWTest. Place FXS_Fountain in a grid of 20 by 20 copies, and then place FXS_Fountain_LW in a second grid of 20 by 20 copies.
Open Tools, then Debug, then Niagara Debugger. In the HUD section, enable Show Overview, and set the Debug Overview dropdown to Performance.
Select each system in the Outliner. Write down the Game Thread Average for the regular version and for the lightweight version.
Turn the overlay off and run the console command stat UNIT. Compare the Frame and Draw values for both grids.
In FXS_Fountain_LW, try to add a dynamic input to a module, and note what happens.
Create a Niagara System named FXS_TA_Scratch from the Fountain template and drag it into the level.
In Particle Update, click the + button and choose New Scratch Pad Module. Confirm that the Scratch Pad panel opens and that an empty module is already in your stack.

In the scratch module, add a float input named Strength. Read Particles.Position, push the particle sideways by Strength * Particles.NormalizedAge, and write the result back to Particles.Position. Click Apply and watch the viewport.

Now open Window > Scratch Pad. Click the + button next to Dynamic Inputs and make a scratch dynamic input that returns a float from a sine of Engine.Time. Attach it to Sprite Size in Initialize Particle.
Right-click the scratch module in the Scratch Script Selector and choose Create Asset. Name the asset NMS_TA_SidePush.
Delete the scratch version from the stack and add the NMS_TA_SidePush asset from the library in its place. Confirm that the effect looks the same.
Add a Set new or existing parameter directly item to the stack. Use it to create a new Particle float parameter that stores the push amount.
